Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette: Michael is a 29-year-old European-American male who works as a salesperson. He has been experiencing significant distress following a traumatic event involving a severe natural disaster, which occurred about six months ago. At the time of the trauma, Michael was hiking in the mountains near his home when an unexpected landslide struck. The force and speed with which it happened left him feeling completely vulnerable and overwhelmed. Since then, he has developed several PTSD symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. Michael vividly recalls the moment the landslide began. He had been walking through a beautiful natural environment, enjoying the peace of being in nature. Suddenly, without warning, the ground beneath him shifted violently, and large boulders started rolling down the mountain. In an instant, he was swept away by the rush of debris and mud. The experience left him feeling both physically and emotionally vulnerable, as if any moment could bring another devastating event. Since that day, Michael has found it challenging to revisit natural environments similar to where the landslide occurred. Simple activities like hiking or even driving through rural areas now trigger intense fear and anxiety. He is constantly on guard in these settings, hyperalert for signs of danger. Even seemingly mundane locations can remind him of his trauma, leading to sudden flashbacks that make him feel as though he is reliving the event. At night, Michael wakes up frequently, driven by an overwhelming need to check whether he is safe. This hypervigilance extends into his daily life, where he feels a constant sense of alertness and watchfulness. He has become increasingly isolated due to these heightened fears, avoiding places that remind him of the traumatic event. His avoidance behaviors have extended beyond just natural environments; he also avoids any conversations or thoughts about what happened. Michael's experience with memory disruptions is also significant. Sometimes, when he recalls the landslide, he feels an intense emotional response without being able to conjure up clear visual memories of the event. He has gaps in his recollection, making it difficult for him to fully process and understand what occurred. When he does remember parts of the event, they bring back the same paralyzing terror he felt at that time. In addition to these symptoms, Michael's sense of self has been profoundly affected. Since the landslide, he feels like he doesn't know himself anymore. The trauma has left him feeling disconnected from his previous identity and goals. He struggles with a pervasive sense that nothing in his life holds any real meaning or purpose. This loss of meaning is compounded by a growing belief that he cannot rely on others for support. Michael's occupation as a salesperson has also been impacted. His avoidance behaviors have led to missed work appointments and cancelled client meetings, particularly if they were scheduled in outdoor locations or areas near nature. He often feels like canceling planned events last minute because of his intense anxiety about being triggered. What finally brought Michael to seek help was the realization that his quality of life had significantly deteriorated. His fear of vulnerability and his inability to find meaning in daily activities had become overwhelming. The mounting consequences of his avoidance behaviors-both professionally and personally-were too much to bear on his own. He is most afraid of losing control over his life completely, but he also hopes that with help, he can regain a sense of stability and meaning. Michael believes that understanding and managing the triggers and symptoms will allow him to reconnect with who he used to be and find value in his experiences once again.
